XX Global Open Synchronous Championship

Season 2022–2023

Leg VI (17 – 27.02.2023)



Notes for the reader:

 

Please familiarise yourself with the question pack before the game.

 

Words in caps (e.g., X, FIRST, IT, DO THIS) should be emphasized when reading out loud. After reading the answer, you should also read out other accepted answers and the commentary to the question. Reading out the name(s) of the author(s) is advisable but not necessary.

 

Additional notes for the reader are placed in square brackets before some of the questions. You must not read them out loud.

 

Phonetic transcriptions of selected words (in square brackets) are put within the text of some questions for the reader’s convenience.

 

Handouts for questions 24 and 26 are placed before the text of the questions. Please give the teams some time to familiarise themselves with the handouts, but do not read them out loud.

 

Good luck!







Round 1.

Edited by: Oleg Mikheev [me-KAY-eff] and Alexander Uskov [oos-KOFF].



The editors would like to thank the following individuals for their help in developing the questions: Maxim Bolonkin [buh-LON-kin], Alexei Boronenko [buh-raw-NEN-caw], Ivan Veselov [veh-seh-LOFF], Nikita Vorobyev [vuh-raw-BYOFF], Natalya Getmanskaya [GET-mahn-sky-uh], Artyom Guletsky [goo-LETS-key], Konstantin Kolomiets [caw-law-me-ETS], Ilya Kukushkin [coo-COOSH-kin], Alexander Pechony [peh-CHOH-ny], Andrei Rud, Sardar Sadykov [sah-DEEK-off], Andrei Skirenko [ski-REN-caw], Alexander Taranik [tah-RAH-nick], Vadim Tukh, Nail Farukshin [far-ROOK-shin], Dmitri Khachaturov [kah-chah-TOOR-off] and Andrei Khromov [KRAW-moff].



Question 1.
The eccentric Lord Berners wrote THIS titled “For A Rich Aunt”, to be played in a lively tempo. Identify THIS using exactly two words.

Answer: Funeral march.
Comment: Lively and happy music does not sound exactly like a typical funeral march. The composer’s joke was that a rich aunt’s death is not particularly depressing, especially if it is you who gets to inherit.

Source:
1. Bryony Jones. The Music of Lord Berners (1883-1950) // https://bit.ly/3lnQj1T // https://i.imgur.com/Ake2NKE.png
Author: Oleg Mikheev.

Question 2.
In a 1932 comic, an inventive boy who does not want to do his homework shows his mother a new composition, which he had been practicing. By a funny coincidence, the author of the comic shares his surname with a certain famous person born in Los Angeles. Identify this surname.



Answer: Cage.

Comment: The boy had composed a musical piece the consists entirely of pauses, without a single sound. The author, Hy Cage, drew this comic two decades before John Cage composed his 4’33.

1. John Biguenet. Silence // http://bit.ly/40SnV84

2. https://i.imgur.com/DsBY8Ct.jpeg

Author: Oleg Mikheev.

Question 3.
On the Bolivian Congress building, THIS DOES IT THAT WAY. One Bolivian politician noted that it emphasises the fact that Bolivia is in the Southern hemisphere and symbolises liberation from the colonial legacy. Which words did we substitute with THIS DOES IT THAT WAY?

Answer: [The] clock goes backwards (accept phrases that mean the same, e.g. with “clock hands”, “turn(s)”, “anti-clockwise”).
Comment: Historically, the “clockwise” direction refers to the way the shadow on a sundial would move in the Northern hemisphere. In the other hemisphere it moves the other way.

Sources:
1. Bolivia congress clock altered to turn anti-clockwise //
2. https://www.bbc.com/news/world-latin-america-28013157
Author: Oleg Mikheev.

Question 4.
The hosts of a certain podcast suggest a concept episode which would be broken into multiple segments, with only one host speaking in each segment. Which film classic is this episode about?

Answer: Rashomon.
Comment: In Akira Kurosawa’s Rashomon, probably for the first time in cinema, one and the same event is shown from the point of view of multiple characters.

Source: подкаст «Крупным планом» (The Close-Up Podcast) // http://bit.ly/3XgjIIu
Author: Alexander Uskov.

Question 5.
In his old years, Norwegian Thor Heyerdahl was obsessed with finding the place where THEY had come from. Among other places, he searched the shores of the Azov Sea. What is the name of the place that THEY inhabit?

Answer: Asgard.
Comment: The Aesir are the main tribe of gods in Norse mythology. With age, Heyerdahl became interested in myths and false etymologies. Looking for the place where the Aesir started their journey north, he made several research trips to Azerbaijan, but did not find anything; then he switched to the Azov Sea and even excavated in the town of Azov in the Rostov region.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thor_Heyerdahl#Revision_of_hypothesis
Author: Oleg Mikheev.

Question 6.
Captain James Kirk from Star Trek was born in Iowa. In one town in Iowa, there is an unusual memorial plaque that says Captain Kirk was born there. What did we substitute in the previous sentence?

Answer: Will be [born].
Comment: Star Trek is set in the future, so the plaque reads: “Future Birthplace of Captain James T. Kirk, March 22, 2228”

Source: https://www.atlasobscura.com/places/captain-james-t-kirk-future-birthplace
Author: Oleg Mikheev.

Question 7.
In order not to exacerbate the 1893 financial crisis, President Grover Cleveland did not publicly admit that he had learned about THIS. Instead, he said he would take some days off to go fishing on a yacht. Cleveland was not THIS himself, although, quite expectedly, 4 out of 45 US presidents were THIS. Identify THIS.

Answer: Cancer (accept non-capitalised).
Comment: The news that the President had cancer could cause panic on Wall Street, so he had his surgery in secret, out of public sight on a friend’s yacht. If we assume (correctly) that births are spread virtually evenly across the year and one’s zodiac sign does not influence one’s chances of becoming a president, then 4 presidents out of 45 is the most expected number for any one sign.

Sources:
1. A Yacht, A Mustache: How A President Hid His Tumor // http://bit.ly/3Ijvtd7
2. http://www.zodiacpage.com/astrology/zodiac-sign-rankings-for-most-world-leaders/
Author: Oleg Mikheev.

Question 8.
A small Australian battalion once had to hold an island against overwhelming Japanese forces. The inventive Australians ended up doing as the locals did, but with a different purpose. What term is used to describe the phenomenon involving such behaviour?

Answer: Cargo cult.
Comment: The Australians defending Goodenough Island built a fake hospital, assembled fake anti-aircraft guns out of logs and used vines to imitate barb wire. The plan worked, and the Australians were able to deter the enemy until reinforcements arrived. This looked like the behaviour of some Melanesian natives who built models of landing strips to attract planes and cargo from the industrial world. It is worth noting that there was also an actual cargo cult on Goodenough Island.

Sources:
1. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Goodenough_Island#Deception
2. Michael W. Young. Goodenough Island Cargo Cults // https://www.jstor.org/stable/40329972
Author: Oleg Mikheev.

Question 9.
In the middle of the 19th century, the young prince Arthur was standing on a small box, when a maid approached him for a moment. The result is seen as one of the earliest examples of THIS. A con man who made THIS had to find his way into his customers’ homes the day before. Identify THIS using two words, one of which is derived from Latin and the other from Greek.

Answer: spirit photo[graph/y] (accept “ghost” instead of “spirit”)
Comment: The long exposure, typical for early photography, created a transparent outline of the maid which looked like a ghost. To fake a photo with the purported ghost of a deceased relative, the con man would steal portraits of such relatives and then either take a shot of his assistant made to look like the deceased person or photograph the portrait itself.

Sources:
1. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_H._Mumler
2. https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Спиритическая_фотография
Author: Alexander Uskov.

Question 10.
Journalist James Morris was worried about his telegraph messages being intercepted by competitors from other papers. Thus, he used coded language that looked like innocent weather reports. For example, “Snow Conditions Bad” would mean success, and “Trouble with Wind” stood for failure. Eventually, the phrase about snow conditions was telegraphed together with coded names of two individuals. Identify any one of these two.

Answer: [Edmund] Hillary (accept Tenzing [Norgay]).
Comment: The 9th British Everest expedition featured a Times journalist. As soon as the mountain was conquered, he gave his message to a Sherpa runner who ran down to the telegraph in the nearest village. As a result, the Times were the first to report on the ascent.

Sources:
1. Stephen Venables. Everest: Summit of Achievement // http://bit.ly/3jBt4Ru //
https://imgur.com/a/7HTICpK
2. Mick Conefrey. Everest 1953: The Epic Story of the First Ascent // http://bit.ly/3jJfsn7
Author: Oleg Mikheev.

Question 11.
In the mid-20th century, a certain cake mix was not very successful, but its sales grew when the manufacturer took egg powder out of the mix. This story is often cited as an example of THIS effect, even before THIS became world famous. Identify THIS.

Answer: IKEA.
Comment: Baking a cake with this mix was easier and quicker than making one from scratch, but some participation in the process was still needed, like adding fresh eggs. The situation when customers put a higher value on products which require some effort is called the “IKEA effect”, because IKEA furniture has to be assembled by the buyer.

Sources:
1. Dan Ariely. Payoff: The Hidden Logic That Shapes Our Motivations //
2. http://bit.ly/3lodPvn // https://i.imgur.com/0P7tMPt.png
Author: Oleg Mikheev.

Question 12.
The basic meaning of the English verb to snip has to do with cutting. What nickname got attached to an unknown man who terrorised Northern Pennsylvania by ambushing girls and snipping locks of their hair?

Answer: Jack the Snipper.
Comment: This nickname referred to Jack the Ripper, who committed bloody murders in London. Like his more sinister predecessor, Jack the Snipper never got caught, and according to some views he did not even exist.

Sources:
1. Ed Lewis. Look Back: Panic swept the Wyoming Valley for ‘Jack the Snipper’ in 1917 //
2. http://bit.ly/3YtDqSg
Author: Oleg Mikheev.



Round 2.

Edited by: Alexei Boronenko [buh-raw-NEN-caw].

The editors would like to thank the following individuals for their help in developing the questions: Stanislav Adaskevich [ah-dass-KEH-vich], Alexander Ignatenkov [ig-nah-TEN-koff], Pavel Kaznacheev [kaz-nah-CHE-yeff], Klim Komissarov [caw-mis-SAHR-off], Alexander Korobeynikov [core-oh-BEY-nick-off], Alexander Kotlyarov [cot-lyah-ROFF], Marina Lagutina [lah-GOO-tee-nuh], Oleg Mikheev [me-KAY-eff], Alexander Pechony [peh-CHOH-ny], Maria Podryadchikova [pod-RYAD-chi-kuh-vuh], Dmitri Rodionov [raw-dee-OH-nuff], Andrei Skirenko [ski-REN-caw], Pavel Stolyarov [staw-lya-ROFF], Svetlana Strelnikova [STRELL-nick-uh-vuh], Vadim Tukh, Nail Farukshin [far-ROOK-shin], Alexander Yakovlev [YAH-kov-leff], Natalia Yakovleva [YAH-kov-leh-vuh].


Question 13.

An autogyro is a type of aircraft with a large propeller, which eventually lost out to the more practical helicopter. The creator of the autogyro, Juan de la Cierva, criticised helicopters even in his final days. It is said that the idea came to his mind after he saw a theatre play. Which novel was the play based on?

Answer: Don Quixote (accept Don Quijote or The Ingenious Gentleman Don Quixote of La Mancha)
Comment: Seeing Don Quixote tilting at the windmills, the Spanish inventor devised a mechanism that creates lift through the effect of aerodynamic forces on a rotor. The aircraft turned out to be less practical or efficient than a helicopter, but de la Cierva never accepted it.

Source: George, A. How Quixote’s Windmills Inspired a Spanish Inventor to Envision Vertical Flight // The Smithsonian Magazine (https://bit.ly/3HB6AI3).
Author: Alexei Boronenko.

Question 14.
A European manager once noticed the progress of the USA national team and said that the team had jumped from THIS to THAT. In fact, the word “THIS” did not arise in the US. Identify THIS and THAT and write them down in the right order.

Answer: Soccer, football.
Comment: Carlos Queiroz said in a slightly patronising way that Americans had outgrown their soccer and now play real football. Although “soccer” is the American term for the sport, the word itself originated in British slang. It was used among British students as a contraction of “association”.

Sources:
1. https://twitter.com/usmntonly/status/1597310420490256385.
2. Soccer // The Oxford English Dictionary (http://bit.ly/3Y8tayZ).
Author: Alexei Boronenko.

Question 15.
In 1925, a documentary about a remote exotic location was produced. In one scene, an inhabitant of this location says that he wants to visit New York. In the next decade, the creators of this documentary made another, more famous film. Name that film.

Answer: King Kong.
Comment: In the documentary by Ernest Schoedsack and Merian Cooper, a Persian nomad wanted to visit New York, but never made it there. Conversely, King Kong made it there, although no-one asked him if he wanted to. The 1933 King Kong begins with a filmmaker setting off on a new trip to film a remote exotic location; the character was based on Schoedsack and Cooper.

Sources:
1. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grass_(1925_film).
2. Cooper, M.C. Grass. — 1925. — p. 53 (https://bit.ly/3Wc1oj9).
3. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Kong_(1933_film).
Author: Alexei Boronenko.

Question 16.
The Schoedsack and Cooper documentary was the first to show the Persian nomads’ way to winter pastures, full of unpredictable dangers. On the poster, THIS was Necessity, and THAT was Fate. Identify THIS and THAT, in any order.

Answer: Screenwriter, director (accept “writer”).
Comment: Back then, ethnographic documentaries were a novelty, and so the advert stressed that the events in the film were a true story.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grass_(1925_film).
Author: Alexei Boronenko.

Question 17.
In a certain literary work, a cat’s bookshelf is shown. On it one can see pun versions of famous American novels, like The Great Catsby or Cat-22. Which 1937 book is shown with its original title?

Answer: Of Mice and Men.
Comment: Both mice and men feature prominently in a cat’s life, so the Steinbeck novella might as well retain its original title.

Source: Crumble, P., Gifford, L. The Cat Wants Cuddles. — Scholastic, 2017. — p. 11 (https://bit.ly/3Yxxt6D).
Author: Nina Semushina.

Question 18.
The first organisation to be described with these two words studied psychology, not warfare. Earlier, these two words were used in slang to mean the brain. Identify these two words, which start with the same letter.

Answer: think tank.

Comment: The phrase, now used to mean analytical and research groups, was initially a slang term for the brain or the head. The first organisation to be called this way had nothing to do with tanks and war in general, and was concerned with Behaviourist psychology (although it was hardly a think tank in the modern sense).

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Think_tank.
Author: Alexei Boronenko.

Question 19.
One series features a British spy in Cold War-era Europe. He is under suspicion of being a traitor. Another character in the same series makes a reference by mentioning the dark side of THIS. Identify THIS using only one noun.

Answer: [the] Wall.
Comment: The spy, who used to work in Berlin, is suspected of being a Soviet spy, i.e. having crossed over to the dark side of the Berlin wall. The “Dark Side of the Wall” is a reference to two Pink Floyd albums and, potentially, to the Dark Side of the Force, as the spy could have joined the enemy.

Sources:
1. Slow Horses (2022). — S2 E1. — 27:50–27:55.
2. Slow Horses (2022). — S2 E2. — 45:00–45:10.
Author: Alexei Boronenko.

Question 20.
Prius Leon is a character in one English-language TV series. He makes up stories for other characters, describштп events that happened to them before. We have omitted some letters in his name. Write it down in its original form.

Answer: Previous [Leon].
Comment: To put a long story short, this odd character makes up stories about other characters and tells them in the “previously on” format.

Source: Rick and Morty. — S6 E7.
Author: Alexei Boronenko.





Question 21.
The author of an 18th-century medical treatise wrote: believing that coffee is harmful is as stupid as thinking that THIS is dangerous to use. The word for THIS in Serbian — «жи́ва» [ZHEE-vah] — is related to the word that means “alive”. Identify THIS.



Answer: Mercury (accept “quicksilver”).
Comment: The author wrote that everyone would eventually accept coffee, just as they had accepted treatments with mercury (along with antimony and tobacco). He was partially right and partially not so much. The words for mercury, or quicksilver, are in many languages linked to how it moves and seems “alive”.

Sources:
1. Moseley, B. A Treatise Concerning the Properties and Effects of Coffee. — 1792. — С. 62 (https://bit.ly/3JJsADw).
2. https://sr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Жива.
Author: Alexei Boronenko.

Question 22.
In 2016 psychiatrist Takahiro Kato suggested setting up support centres for X’s in places, so to say, inhabited by Y’s. Identify X’s and Y’s using words of foreign origin.

Answer: Hikikomori, Pokemon[s] (also accept “hikki”).
Comment: Pokemon Go, a very popular game at the time, invited its users to leave home. Among them were not only typical introverts, but also the so-called hikikomori, young people living as recluses. The psychiatrist saw this as an opportunity to help them socialise and to support their mental health.

Source: Kato, T.A. et al. New Game Software (Pokémon Go) May Help Youth With Severe Social Withdrawal, Hikikomori. — Psychiatry Research. — 2016 (https://bit.ly/3RwTe4h).
Author: Alexei Boronenko.

Question 23.
A British doctor once made a guess that an invited patient at his lecture was a soldier. At first the patient lied that he had never been in the military, but after a more thorough examination a tattooed grade was found. What did we substitute with the word “grade”?

Answer: [letter] D.
Comment: Sherlock Holmes’s prototype, Scottish physician George Bell, loved showing off for his students and during his lectures not only diagnosed the invited individual, but also reconstructed their biography through less noticeable details. When a new invitee said that Bell “read” him wrong, the physician did not believe him. In fact, the patient was ashamed to admit that he had indeed been a deserter and had a D tattoo on his chest. Although this is not always a shameful act. In many countries, a D is a school grade.

Source: Joseph Bell. An Appreciation By An Old Friend. — Edinburgh, 1913. — p. 20–21 (https://bit.ly/3xa3zd8).
Author: Alexei Boronenko.





Question 24.
Handout:
[Aging and Youth]


On the handout you can see the current name of a legislative committee in Pennsylvania. It used to have a slightly different name. The previous name was discarded when they found it sounded like what term?

Answer: euthanasia.
Comment: The committee used to be called Youth and Aging, which was too close to “euthanasia”, and the committee dealing with the issues of seniors did not want to have that association.

Source: Youth and Aging // Weird Universe (https://bit.ly/3You89L).
Author: Alexei Boronenko.





Round 3.



Edited by: Andrei Skirenko [ski-REN-caw].



The editors would like to thank the following individuals for their help in developing the questions: Alexei Boronenko [buh-raw-NEN-caw], Artyom Guletsky [goo-LETS-key], Tatyana Davidiuk [duh-vee-DUKE], Maxim Degtyaryov [dig-tyah-RYOFF], Mikhail Kalinin [cah-LEAN-in], Irina Ladvischenko [lud-VISH-chen-caw], Ilya Matyashin [mah-TYA-shin], Oleg Mikheev [me-KAY-eff], Maria Podryadchikova [pod-RYAD-chi-kuh-vuh], Gleb Popov [puh-POFF], Andrei Rud and Vadim Tukh.



Question 25.
The first Europeans to visit Japan tried to spread ideas beyond religious ones. A historian has noted that the Japanese, who were completely sure of their own superiority, liked THIS most of all. Identify THIS.

Answer: [the] heliocentric system [of the world/Universe] (accept “Copernican/Copernicus’s system”, or “model” instead of “system”)
Comment: The Land of the Rising Sun, ruled by an emperor descended from the sun goddess, appreciated the idea of the Sun as the centre of the world and the rest orbiting around it.

Source: В. Елисееф, Д. Елисеефф. Японская цивилизация. (V. Elisseeff, D. Elisseeff, Japanese Civilisation) С. 225; http://bit.ly/3x2rQBQ
Author: Igor Laptev

Question 26.
Handout:
[類似 [ruiji] — similar, alike]

Norman Caruso cites the word “ruiji” to explain the choice of a name. Which name?

Answer: Luigi (accept ルイージ)
Comment: In the development of Super Mario Bros., the creators had to choose a name for Mario’s brother, who was at first distinguishable only by the colour of his clothes. For the game designer Shigeru Miyamoto, the Japanese approximation of the name Luigi — with a different spelling, but the same sound as “ruiji” — became one of the arguments for this choice.

Sources:
1. How the Mario Characters Got Their Names; https://youtu.be/aTyxQfpOEbE?t=369
2. https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/類似#Japanese
Author: Andrei Skirenko

Question 27.
The first model of Rubik’s cube was not made of plastic. Speaking about his toy finding a life of its own, Erno Rubik compared himself… to who?

Answer: [Mister] Geppetto (accept “Papa Carlo”)
Comment: His first puzzle was made of wooden cubes. The wooden boy Pinocchio, created by Geppetto, also became independent very soon and overshadowed his father. As Rubik lived in Socialist Hungary, you might have chosen a different name for the woodcarver, the one from the Soviet Russian adaptation of the book. We will accept this answer too.

Sources:
1. Э. Рубик. Кубик Рубика: За гранями головоломки, или Природа творческой мысли (E. Rubik, Cubed: The Puzzle of Us All); http://bit.ly/3RAdjXk
2. https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Кубик_Рубика
Author: Andrei Skirenko

Question 28.
Jean Delumeau writes that the Dutchman’s invention was especially attractive for the Spanish and the Portuguese, who were interested in the tropics. Identify this Dutchman.

Answer: [Gerardus] Mercator (accept “[Gerhard/Geert] Kremer”)
Comment: His map projection showed the tropical latitudes with minimal distortion, which was especially useful for colonisers and explorers of the tropics.

Source: Ж. Делюмо. Цивилизация Возрождения (J. Delumeau, La Civilisation de la Renaissance). С. 193; http://bit.ly/3HYvyTd
Author: Igor Laptev

Question 29.
Legend has it that in the 1920s Conrad Hilton once took a look at a bottle of… which beverage?

Answer: cognac (accept “brandy”)
Comment: Cognac labels use stars to indicate quality. One explanation says that the creator of the hotel chain borrowed the five-star system from these labels.

Sources:
1. Market Power №3 2022
2. Conrad Hilton Biography: The History of Hilton Hotels Corporation; https://bit.ly/3X9enT9
3. Как Конрад Хилтон смог навсегда изменить гостиничный мир, просто изучая людские особенности; http://bit.ly/3HYO1iy
4. История гостиничного бизнеса. Кто придумал звездную градацию отелей и при чем здесь коньяк; https://bit.ly/3JJWgA4
Author: Andrei Skirenko

Question 30.
Medieval thinker Michael Psellos [sell-OSS] noted that the eye is convex, and thus he explained the order of THIS and THAT. Identify THIS and THAT.

Answer: lightning, thunder (accept in any order)
Comment: The eye is convex, while the eye is concave — and this is how the 11th-century philosopher explained why light comes before sound. The physical nature of this process was little known at the time.

Source: А. Гийу. Византийская цивилизация (A. Guillou, La civilisation byzantine). С. 352; http://bit.ly/3JJcnOs
Author: Igor Laptev

Question 31.
The ilkhan Gaykhatu, who ruled in Iran in late 13th century, was accused of wastefulness. To cope with the problem, Gaykhatu, a first for West Asia, tried to introduce THIS, but it only led to revolts. Identify THIS.

Answer: paper money (accept “notes”, “bills”, “chao”)
Comment: Gaykhatu loved giving lavish gifts, and malcontents started spreading rumours that his gold stores were emptying. His attempt to introduce Chinese-style paper money, called chao, sparked fierce resistance and became one of the causes of his downfall. The word chao became a synonym for worthless currency. There is a version of the story in which the khan is persuaded to use paper money by Marco Polo who at the time was indeed traversing Iran on his way back from China.

Sources:
1. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jiaochao
2. Г. Потапов. Персидская империя. Иран с древнейших времён до наших дней
3. А. Гаркавец. Марко Поло по прозвищу миллион и его «Книга о разнообразии мира»; http://bit.ly/3lhbyCb
Author: Andrei Skirenko

Question 32.
The inhabitants of Dahomey raided their neighbours. Knowing about one Dahomey superstition, the Tofinu people built a village which is often called African THIS. Identify THIS.

Answer: Venice.
Comment: The village of Ganvié stands in water, and people move across it on boats. Europeans like comparing any settlement of this kind to Venice. The slaver raiders had a superstition preventing them from stepping into the water or even crossing it in vessels, so the inhabitants felt protected in the lake. Now the place is a UNESCO Heritage Site.

Sources:
1. Д. Бондаренко. Трансатлантическая работорговля глазами африканцев // Родина слонов №328; https://youtu.be/7-7L2lzCcdE?t=1545
2. The Tofinu people: the fishermen of Benin; https://youtu.be/QEguajkh4tU
3. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganvie
Author: Andrei Skirenko

Question 33.
Who wrote a letter to his father with accusations of treating him like a parasite, or “das Ungeziefer” [dass oon-get-SEE-fer]?

Answer: [Franz] Kafka
Comment: This word was apparently common in their family usage, and it was used by Kafka to describe the insect creature in his Metamorphosis, written 7 years before the letter. Although the literary scholar Maxim Zhuk (lit. Beetle) warns against treating the novella as only a metaphor for his row with his father.

Sources:
1. Ф. Кафка. Письмо отцу (F. Kafka, Brief an den Vater); http://bit.ly/3Y6FPlL
2. https://de.wikisource.org/wiki/Brief_an_den_Vater
Author: Andrei Skirenko

Question 34.
Sofia Bagdasarova [bug-dah-SAH-raw-vuh] writes that on Renaissance coins and medals those people who had passed away usually DID THIS. One workers’ party had a magazine called “DO THIS”. What did we substitute with DO THIS?

Answer: Look left.
Comment: As viewers were used to reading left-to-right, a face looking left was seen as looking into the past, because deceased people have no future. The Look Left magazine was launched by the Irish Workers’ Party, but by now has become an independent left-wing paper.

Sources:
1. С. Багдасарова. Гений по имени Пизанелло и октябрятская звездочка; http://bit.ly/3RDVNS1
2. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Workers’_Party_(Ireland)
3. https://www.lookleft.ie
Author: Andrei Skirenko

Question 35.
Oscar Peterson was a famous jazz musician, but in the USSR he was unknown. A Soviet journalist who showed Peterson his column about the musician’s tour, later remembered that it was the first time Peterson had seen such THIS. Identify THIS using two words.

Answer: small print (accept “small font”)
Comment: The Canadian star was used to being the object of attention, so being unpopular really surprised him. By the way, the author of this small-print column was Sergei Dovlatov [dove-LAH-toff].

Sources:
1. А. Рондарев. Эпоха распада
2. С. Довлатов. Чёрная музыка; http://bit.ly/3xj4bNH
Author: Andrei Skirenko

Question 36.
The recording of Yes album Union brought together members from various line-ups of the band. Rick Wakeman said that working together resulted only in disappointment. What nickname did he give to the album?

Answer: Onion
Comment: Wakeman made a pun on the album title, hinting at something that brings forth tears. We hope that this tournament did not bring you to tears.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_(Yes_album)
Author: Andrei Skirenko
